A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, retaining the reconstruction-hypernetwork framework, continuous-message bound, and moons examples despite substantial expansion and retitling. All 11 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: Section 6 and Figures 2–3 report original moons experiments, including test errors, computed generalization bounds, and learned decision boundaries.

after.justification: Sections 4.2–4.4 report original moons, MNIST, and CIFAR100 experiments. Appendices C and H additionally report numerical bound comparisons.

M1.justification: Beyond retaining the sample/message/reconstructor pipeline, v2 revises the stated continuous-message training objective from v1's deterministic Equation 3 to an expectation over Gaussian-perturbed messages in Equation 9, with a corresponding latent-only objective in Equation 4. Definition 4.1 also adds multiclass label encoding. Binary STP-to-DeepSet renaming and the zero-compression-set special case alone are not new methods.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only transformed synthetic moons tasks. v2 retains moons and adds MNIST classification with 100/200/300 pixel swaps, binary MNIST class-pair tasks, and binary CIFAR100 tasks, substantially expanding domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: v1 has no external baseline experiments. v2 Tables 1–2 add comparisons with Pentina and Lampert (2014), Amit and Meir (2018), Guan and Lu (2022; kl and Catoni variants), Zakerinia et al. (2024), and an opaque-encoder control. Rezazadeh (2022) additionally participates in the binary-task comparison.

E3.justification: The moons generation procedure and 300-training/100-test-task split remain unchanged. New protocols specify 10 training and 20 test tasks for pixel-swapped MNIST, and class-based partitions with 34/50 test tasks for binary MNIST/CIFAR100. Appendix C also introduces controlled numerical bound comparisons at m = 10000, delta = 0.01, and KL values of 100 and 10000.

E4.justification: v1's compression-size/message-size sensitivity heatmaps are removed. v2 adds latent-coordinate interventions in Figure 3, the opaque-encoder control and noisy-task comparison, numerical analysis of full-dataset versus complement-set bounds in Appendix C, and alternative-bound comparisons in Table 4. The original compression-point decision-boundary examples survive as Figure 4.

E5.justification: v1 reports task-averaged moons results without empirical uncertainty estimates. v2 Tables 1, 2, and 4 introduce 95% confidence intervals for bounds and test errors across 20, 34, or 50 test tasks. This establishes new cross-task uncertainty reporting, not increased training repetitions; neither version specifies repeated-training counts or seeds.

E6.justification: The quantitative moons sweep in v1 Figure 2 disappears, while v2 Tables 1, 2, and 4 add extensive benchmark and alternative-bound results. For example, binary-MNIST SCH+ reports a bound of 0.280 ± 0.148 and test error of 0.155 ± 0.109. These are newly reported results under added settings, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: v2 substantially extends v1's continuous-message theorem and corollaries. Appendices B–D derive general bounds over joint compression-set/message distributions and rederive the retained continuous-message result. Theorem 2.5 and Appendices E–F add disintegrated bounds for a single sampled predictor, with proofs and corollaries. Several bounded-loss corollaries are also replaced by sub-Gaussian formulations.

C1.justification: v1 claims a learned reconstruction function, a continuous-message compression bound, and promising preliminary toy results. v2 broadens the central contribution to learning model representations across PAC-Bayes, sample compression, and their hybrid. Its introduction and conclusion additionally claim that these representations support tight bounds across differing tasks where existing PAC-Bayesian meta-learning approaches struggle.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive applicability distinctions: noisy MNIST tasks are described as unsuitable for its task-representation approach, whereas binary tasks expose limitations of shared-prior methods. Appendix C explains why full-dataset bounds help only in unfavorable high-loss/high-KL regimes. v1's interpretation of the size sweep and suggestion to regularize the KL term are removed.

D1.justification: Appendix H adds learning-rate, network-architecture, compression-size, and message-size search grids for the image experiments; Table 3 supplies selected representation sizes. Existing moons architecture, GPU, optimizer, initialization, and 200-epoch information are largely retained or relocated. However, v1's explicit batch size of 20 is omitted, without evidence that the actual batch size changed.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around PAC-Bayesian meta-learning, information bottlenecks, and disintegrated bounds, adding works such as Pentina and Lampert, Amit and Meir, Tishby and Zaslavsky, and Viallard et al. It contrasts latent-space distributions with prior approaches and adds an Appendix C critique of an earlier theorem's scope. v1's Pick-to-learn discussion and citation disappear.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around model representations and three theoretical frameworks. Theory and architecture sections are reorganized, terminology is standardized into PBH/SCH/PBSCH variants, and Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix G. This substantially changes the narrative beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, with new tables, architecture diagrams, latent-space plots, and appendix bound-comparison heatmaps. v1 Figure 1 is redrawn, Figure 3 is retained as v2 Figure 4, and Figure 2 is removed. Appendix G relocates the algorithm and redisplays architecture schematics.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's important limitation of toy-only evidence without external comparisons through image-task benchmarks, an informative opaque-encoder control, uncertainty reporting, and explicit discussion of failure conditions. The expanded theoretical derivations and bound comparisons also strengthen the contribution. These gains outweigh losing the moons size sweep and some reporting weaknesses. The superiority language remains too broad: Table 1 reports a tighter 300-swap bound for Zakerinia et al. (0.149) than SCH+ (0.177).
